body.heading: Sleep starts before the pillow
paragraphs: Bodies do not switch off like lamps. The transition from a bright, busy, screen-lit evening to sleep is a slope, not a step, and the last hour of the day is where that slope is built. People who “cannot switch off” at night are often trying to brake from full speed at the bedroom door.

A wind-down routine is simply a repeated sequence that tells your system, in several languages at once, that the day is ending: dimmer light, slower activities, fewer inputs, a body getting comfortable.

body.heading: Design yours from pleasure, not rules
paragraphs: The classic mistake is copying a stern routine from the internet — no screens, herbal tea, journaling, meditation — and abandoning it within the week because none of it felt like you. Start instead from what already relaxes you: a shower, a chapter of a novel, music, stretching, preparing tomorrow’s clothes, a slow cup of something warm.

Chain three or four of those into a loose order and start them at roughly the same time each night. Loose matters: a wind-down that requires perfect conditions will collapse on exactly the busy evenings when you need it most.

body.heading: Handle the phone honestly
paragraphs: For most people the phone is the wind-down’s main saboteur — not because of any single property, but because it is interesting, bright and infinite. You do not need a ban. Try charging it outside the bedroom, or giving it a bedtime fifteen minutes before yours, with the last stretch of the evening deliberately analogue.

If sleep regularly refuses to come despite a decent wind-down, or poor sleep is affecting your days, that is worth raising with a doctor. This article offers general habits, not a diagnosis — some sleep problems have specific causes and specific help.

takeaway: Build the last hour of the day from things you genuinely enjoy, and let repetition do the rest.
